title: A Boy with a Flying Squirrel (Henry Pelham)

image.credit: Photograph via Wikimedia Commons (John Singleton Copley - A Boy with a Flying Squirrel (Henry Pelham) - Google Art Project.jpg)

source.label: Wikipedia: “After becoming well-established as a portrait painter of the wealthy in colonial New England, he moved to London in 1774”
Wikipedia: “The painting is a profile portrait of Henry Pelham seated at a table”

highlight.text: lett it be Painted in oil, and make it a rule to Paint in that way as much as Posible, for Oil Painting has the superiority over all other Painting.
highlight.lead: Benjamin West, after seeing the picture in London, urged Copley to give up crayons:

source.author: Benjamin West
source.title: Benjamin West to Copley, London, 4 August 1766, in Letters & Papers of John Singleton Copley and Henry Pelham, 1739–1776
source.publisher: Massachusetts Historical Society (1914), via Internet Archive

work.text: its excellence as a work of the highest merit established Copley's European reputation more than a century ago

source.author: Martha Babcock Amory
source.title: The Domestic and Artistic Life of John Singleton Copley, R.A.

work.text: The art historian Jennifer Roberts believed A Boy with a Flying Squirrel to be "the most consequential painting Copley had yet produced in America". It was Copley's first major noncommissioned work and first exhibition painting.

source.author: Wikipedia contributors
source.title: A Boy with a Flying Squirrel

moment.text: He observed a little Hardness in the Drawing, Coldness in the Shades, An over minuteness, all which Example would correct. "But still," he added, "it is a wonderful Picture to be sent by a Young Man who was never out of New England, and had only some bad Copies to study."
moment.lead: Captain R. G. Bruce passes on Joshua Reynolds’s verdict from the London exhibition:

source.author: Joshua Reynolds, as reported by R. G. Bruce
source.title: Captain R. G. Bruce to Copley, London, 4 August 1766, in Letters & Papers of John Singleton Copley and Henry Pelham, 1739–1776
source.publisher: Massachusetts Historical Society (1914), via Internet Archive

moment.text: It was remarkd the Picture was too lind. this I confess I was concious of my self and think with You that it is the natural result of two great presition in the out line

source.author: John Singleton Copley
source.title: Copley to Benjamin West, Boston, 12 November 1766, in Letters & Papers of John Singleton Copley and Henry Pelham, 1739–1776
source.publisher: Massachusetts Historical Society (1914), via Internet Archive

matters.text: I confess I am under some apprehension of its not being so much esteem'd as I could wish … I can truly say if I know my own heart I am less anxious to enjoy than deserve applause.

matters.text: Copley and Pelham held a close and affectionate relationship, as evidenced by a volume of correspondence between the two published in 1914.
